title: Module 4: Section properties, bending theory and member shape
shortTitle: Section properties, bending theory and member shape
whyItMatters: This is one of your most important modules. Cross-sectional shape (A, I, Z_el, W_pl, i) explains why I-beams are shaped the way they are, why section depth dominates stiffness and strength, and why orienting a section on its weak axis can be catastrophic.
introduction: Covers centroids and composite areas, second moment of area I and the parallel-axis theorem, elastic section modulus Z = I/y, Engineer’s bending equation σ = My/I = M/Z, plastic section modulus W_pl and plastic hinge formation, radius of gyration i = √(I/A), and major vs minor axis efficiency of Universal Beams.
objectives: Calculate centroids, second moment of area I, elastic section modulus Z, and bending stress σ for rectangular and composite sections (Examples 4.1 and 4.2).
Compare major-axis and minor-axis properties of I-sections and explain why section orientation and restraint matter (Example 4.3).
Distinguish elastic and plastic stress distributions, plastic modulus, shape factor, and why local buckling or LTB can prevent full plastic resistance (Example 4.4).
learningGate: Calculate I, Z, and bending stress for simple sections without hesitation.,Use the parallel-axis theorem (I = Σ(I_0 + A·d²)) accurately for built-up sections.,Explain major and minor axes and the danger of loading a UB about its minor axis.,Explain why I-sections are structurally efficient in bending.,Distinguish second moment of area I, elastic section modulus Z, and plastic section modulus W_pl.,Explain why choosing a deeper beam is usually far more effective than simply specifying a higher steel grade when deflection governs.

topics.title: Centroids, Second Moment of Area I & Parallel-Axis Theorem
topics.summary: Covers area centroids, neutral axis location in elastic bending, I = bd³/12 for rectangles (Example 4.1), and the parallel-axis theorem I = I_self + A·d² for composite/built-up shapes (Example 4.2).
subtopics: Area A, first moment of area, and centroid location y_bar = Σ(A_i y_i) / ΣA_i
Why the elastic neutral axis passes through the centroid under pure bending
Second moment of area I = bd³/12 for a rectangle and why units are mm⁴
Parallel-axis theorem: I_xx = Σ(I_0,i + A_i d_i²) for flanges and asymmetric sections (Example 4.2)
Radius of gyration i = √(I/A) and its role in column buckling slenderness
learningObjectives: Calculate centroids and second moments of area for rectangles and built-up sections.
Explain why the A·d² parallel-axis term makes I-section flanges so effective.

questions.prompt: As the applied bending moment on a thin-walled steel I-beam increases beyond first yield of the extreme fibres toward the full plastic stress block, what physical instability can prevent the section from reaching its full plastic moment resistance M_pl = W_pl·f_y?
options: The member is verified solely for Ultimate Limit State cross-sectional yield resistance at midspan while relying on friction alone at the bearings to resist horizontal thermal expansion, wind drag, and notional lateral equivalent forces

The structural analysis models the joint as a frictionless pin for vertical gravity load takedown but simultaneously assumes full rotational fixity when evaluating lateral storey drift and global second-order sway stability
Plastic hinges can only form in brittle materials like glass

High compressive strains in the yielded flange/web can trigger local plate buckling (Class 3 or 4 section), or an unrestrained compression flange can buckle sideways and twist (Lateral Torsional Buckling) before full plastification develops
questions.explanation: Reaching and rotating at M_pl requires the compression elements to be sufficiently stocky (Class 1 or 2) to sustain compressive yield strains without local buckling, and the beam to be laterally restrained against LTB.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why I-sections are structurally efficient in bending (Module 4 Gate)
questions.prompt: Why is an I-section much more efficient in major-axis bending than a solid rectangular bar of the exact same cross-sectional area (and weight per metre)?
options: Because the web carries 100% of the bending moment and the flanges carry 100% of the vertical shear, assuming that because the maximum principal tensile stress under pure shear equals the uniaxial yield strength according to the Rankine maximum normal stress hypothesis, which governs brittle fracture in unreinforced cast iron and uncracked plain concrete elements rather than ductile structural steel

Because elastic bending stress increases linearly with distance from the neutral axis, so placing most of the steel area in two flanges far from the neutral axis maximises the A·d² parallel-axis contribution to I and Z, while a thin web suffices to keep the flanges apart and carry shear
Because material near the neutral axis carries the highest bending stress
Because I-sections have a higher Young’s modulus E than rectangular bars
questions.explanation: Material near the neutral axis is lightly stressed in bending; moving mass to the extreme fibres maximises lever arm and second moment of area per kilogram of steel.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a deeper beam beats a higher steel grade when deflection governs (Module 4 Gate)
questions.prompt: A steel floor beam passes bending strength checks in S275 steel, but fails the serviceability deflection limit by 35%. Why is choosing a slightly deeper beam section effective, whereas changing the steel grade from S275 to S355 does not solve the deflection problem?
questions.assumptions: Final requirement of the Module 4 Learning Gate.
options: S355 steel has a lower Young’s modulus E than S275 steel, assuming that it redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface
Deeper beams always weigh three times more than shallower beams

Elastic deflection depends on flexural stiffness EI (not yield strength f_y); increasing depth increases I roughly with the cube/square of depth, whereas changing from S275 to S355 leaves E (210 GPa) and I completely unchanged

It eliminates vertical shear deformation across the web depth by forcing the neutral axis to remain coincident with the geometric centroid of the uncracked transformed section throughout both construction and permanent service stages
questions.explanation: In δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI), f_y does not appear at all! Only geometry (I) or support/span arrangement can reduce elastic deflection for a given material E.

resources: Hibbeler Mechanics of Materials: centroids, moments of inertia, bending.

moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: Calculate I for 75 × 225 mm rectangular section (Example 4.1)
moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: Calculate the major-axis second moment of area I = bd³/12 for a 75 mm × 225 mm rectangular timber beam in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.
moduleAssessmentQuestions.assumptions: Rectangle bent about its strong axis.
moduleAssessmentQuestions.explanation: I = 75 × 225³ / 12 = 71.191 × 10⁶ mm⁴. moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: Calculate bending stress at an interior point y from the neutral axis
moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: A symmetric beam with second moment of area I = 80 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and overall depth 300 mm (so y_max = 150 mm) is subjected to a sagging moment M = 40 kN·m. Calculate the longitudinal bending stress σ at a point located y = 60 mm below the neutral axis, in N/mm².
moduleAssessmentQuestions.assumptions: At the extreme fibre (y = 150 mm), σ_max = 40×150/80 = 75 N/mm².
moduleAssessmentQuestions.explanation: σ(y) = M × y / I = (40 × 10⁶ N·mm × 60 mm) / (80 × 10⁶ mm⁴) = 30.0 N/mm² (tension). Step-by-step verification for "Calculate bending stress at an interior point y from the neutral axis": confirm that all input quantities are converted into consistent SI metric units before substitution, evaluate the governing equilibrium or constitutive equation to obtain 30 N/mm², and cross-check the magnitude and sign against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 4 (Section Properties, Elastic & Plastic Bending Stress).

moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: Calculate extreme fibre stresses in an unsymmetrical T-section
moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: An unsymmetrical cast-iron or concrete T-beam has second moment of area I = 120 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Its neutral axis lies 80 mm below the top fibre and 160 mm above the bottom fibre. Under a sagging moment of M = 30 kN·m, calculate the maximum tensile stress at the bottom fibre in N/mm².
moduleAssessmentQuestions.assumptions: In an unsymmetrical section, the fibre furthest from the centroidal neutral axis experiences the largest elastic bending stress.
moduleAssessmentQuestions.explanation: σ_bot = M × y_bot / I = (30 × 10⁶ × 160) / (120 × 10⁶) = 40.0 N/mm² tension (while the top fibre has σ_top = 30 × 80 / 120 = 20.0 N/mm² compression).

moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: Explain why the neutral axis passes through the centroid in pure elastic bending
moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: In pure elastic bending (with zero axial force N = 0) of a homogeneous beam, why must the neutral axis pass through the geometric centroid of the cross-section?
moduleAssessmentQuestions.assumptions: Note: once a non-symmetric section yields plastically, the plastic neutral axis (equal area axis) shifts away from the elastic centroid!
options: The member is verified solely for Ultimate Limit State cross-sectional yield resistance at midspan while relying on friction alone at the bearings to resist horizontal thermal expansion, wind drag, and notional lateral equivalent forces
Because the centroid is always at half the overall depth even for a T-section

The design substitutes the characteristic 95th-percentile material strength in place of the 5th-percentile characteristic strength and omits the combination factor ψ_0 when superimpose-combining independent variable wind and imposed floor actions

Because longitudinal normal stress varies linearly with distance y from the neutral axis (σ = E·κ·y), so setting the resultant axial force ∫ σ dA = E·κ ∫ y dA = 0 requires the first moment of area about the neutral axis to be zero
moduleAssessmentQuestions.explanation: Zero first moment of area ∫ y dA = 0 is the exact definition of the centroidal axis. Engineering synthesis for "Explain why the neutral axis passes through the centroid in pure elastic bending": always trace the complete load path from point of application to the foundations, ensure compatibility between analysis boundary assumptions and physical site detailing, and verify against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 4 (Section Properties, Elastic & Plastic Bending Stress).
moduleAssessmentQuestions.citation: Parallel Axis Theorem, Elastic/Plastic Section Analysis & BS EN 1993-1-1 Cl. 6.2.5
hints: Consider the physical load path, equilibrium boundary conditions, and deformation compatibility for "Explain why the neutral axis passes through the centroid in pure elastic bending". Distinguish carefully between ULS strength/stability checks and SLS deflection/cracking behaviour.
Engineering principle check: eliminate options that violate static equilibrium, ignore construction-stage instability, or confuse elastic stiffness (E·I) with material yield strength (f_y).

By assuming a uniform linear-elastic stress distribution across the gross flange and web elements while neglecting rotational restraint compatibility, ecc.
By taking the mean 50th-percentile material stiffness modulus together with a fully fixed rotational boundary condition at both ends, thereby ignoring.

moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: State the core assumptions of Engineer’s Simple Bending Theory (σ = My/I)
moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: Which of the following is a foundational kinematic assumption of Euler-Bernoulli (Engineer’s) bending theory σ = My/I?
moduleAssessmentQuestions.assumptions: Note: in very deep beams (span/depth < 2 to 3), shear deformation causes non-linear stress distribution so simple beam theory no longer holds.
options: Cross-sections warp freely and normal stress is constant over the depth, assuming that the member is verified solely for Ultimate Limit State cross-sectional yield resistance at midspan while relying on friction alone at the bearings to resist horizontal thermal expansion, wind drag, and notional lateral equivalent forces
The beam depth must be greater than its span (deep beam action)
The material must be fully yielded across its entire depth

Plane cross-sections normal to the beam axis before bending remain plane and normal to the deformed axis after bending (yielding a linear strain distribution ε = y/R), and the material is homogeneous and linearly elastic
moduleAssessmentQuestions.explanation: Plane sections remain plane gives linear strain ε ∝ y; combined with Hooke’s law σ = Eε, this produces the linear stress distribution σ = My/I. moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: Calculate combined axial and bending stress at an extreme fibre
moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: A rectangular steel strut of area A = 4,000 mm² and elastic section modulus Z = 200,000 mm³ carries a concentric axial compression force N = 240 kN and a bending moment M = 10 kN·m. Using elastic superposition (ignoring second-order buckling amplification), calculate the maximum compressive stress at the extreme fibre in N/mm².
moduleAssessmentQuestions.assumptions: Elastic superposition σ = N/A ± M/Z.
moduleAssessmentQuestions.explanation: σ_axial = N / A = 240,000 / 4,000 = 60 N/mm² (compression). σ_bending = M / Z = 10,000,000 / 200,000 = 50 N/mm². Maximum compression = 60 + 50 = 110 N/mm² (minimum stress on opposite face = 60 − 50 = 10 N/mm² compression).

moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: Identify why a square hollow section (SHS) resists torsion and minor-axis bending better than an I-section
moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: Why is a closed Square Hollow Section (SHS) or Circular Hollow Section (CHS) often preferred over an open Universal Beam (UB) for a freestanding unbraced compression post or a member subjected to torsion?
moduleAssessmentQuestions.assumptions: Connects member shape to structural application.
options: An SHS/CHS has equal second moment of area and radius of gyration about both axes (I_y = I_z, no weak minor axis) and a closed cell wall that provides vastly superior St Venant torsional stiffness compared to an open I-section

By applying the unfactored characteristic Serviceability Limit State action combination directly to the gross cross-sectional area without accounting for partial material safety factors, second-order geometric imper.
Open I-sections have higher torsional stiffness than closed box sections

By taking the mean 50th-percentile material stiffness modulus together with a fully fixed rotational boundary condition at both ends, thereby ignoring connection flexibility, long-term creep deformation, and d.
moduleAssessmentQuestions.explanation: Open sections made of thin rectangles have very low torsional constant J = Σ(b·t³/3) and a weak minor axis z-z, whereas closed hollow sections resist torsion by shear flow around the enclosed area and have symmetric flexural stiffness.
moduleAssessmentQuestions.citation: Parallel Axis Theorem, Elastic/Plastic Section Analysis & BS EN 1993-1-1 Cl. 6.2.5
hints: Consider the physical load path, equilibrium boundary conditions, and deformation compatibility for "Identify why a square hollow section (SHS) resists torsion and minor-axis bending better than an I-section". Distinguish carefully between ULS strength/stability checks and SLS deflection/cracking behaviour.
Engineering principle check: eliminate options that violate static equilibrium, ignore construction-stage instability, or confuse elastic stiffness (E·I) with material yield strength (f_y).

moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: Calculate shape factor of a solid rectangular section
moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: For any solid rectangular cross-section of breadth b and depth d, calculate the geometric shape factor W_pl / Z_el = (bd²/4) / (bd²/6).
moduleAssessmentQuestions.assumptions: Shows that a rectangular section has 50% reserve moment capacity beyond first yield, whereas an I-section has ~15% reserve because most of its area is already concentrated in the outer flanges.
moduleAssessmentQuestions.explanation: (bd²/4) / (bd²/6) = 6 / 4 = 1.50. Step-by-step verification for "Calculate shape factor of a solid rectangular section": confirm that all input quantities are converted into consistent SI metric units before substitution, evaluate the governing equilibrium or constitutive equation to obtain 1.5 ratio, and cross-check the magnitude and sign against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 4 (Section Properties, Elastic & Plastic Bending Stress).
moduleAssessmentQuestions.citation: Parallel Axis Theorem, Elastic/Plastic Section Analysis & BS EN 1993-1-1 Cl. 6.2.5
hints: Identify the governing equilibrium or mechanics equation for "Calculate shape factor of a solid rectangular section" and convert all given dimensions and loads into consistent SI units (N, mm, or kN, m) before calculating.

moduleAssessmentQuestions.learningObjective: Recognise consequences of cutting holes in I-beam flanges vs web at midspan
moduleAssessmentQuestions.prompt: A services contractor asks to drill a large cable hole at midspan of a heavily loaded simply supported steel I-beam. Which location is far more damaging to the beam’s bending resistance, and why?
moduleAssessmentQuestions.assumptions: Practical site engineering judgement.
options: Cutting a hole at the neutral axis of the web at midspan reduces bending resistance to zero

Cutting the tension or compression flange at midspan is far more damaging because the flanges sit at y_max where bending stress and the A·d² contribution to Z are greatest, whereas a small hole centred on the neutral axis of the web removes material where bending stress is near zero
Flanges carry zero stress at midspan so cutting them has no effect

Because Eurocode partial safety factors for resistance incorporate a statistical log-normal coefficient of variation for hot-rolled plate thickness tolerances, mill rolling residual stresses, and out-of-straightness bow imperfections across the member length
moduleAssessmentQuestions.explanation: At midspan of a UDL beam, M is maximum and V is zero; removing flange area directly reduces Z where bending stress is peak, whereas the neutral axis at mid-depth has σ ≈ 0 (though any web opening must still be checked for local Vierendeel/shear action).
moduleAssessmentQuestions.citation: Parallel Axis Theorem, Elastic/Plastic Section Analysis & BS EN 1993-1-1 Cl. 6.2.5
